Lancelin locals say they are done waiting for the Government to help mitigate coastal erosion threatening the town’s pub and caravan park, launching a fundraiser to build a rock seawall themselves.

The owners and operators of Lancelin Sands Hotel, a favourite beachfront pub 125km north of Perth, launched the GoFundMe after recent severe weather brought the shoreline just seven metres from the venue, compared to 15 metres in March.

They say $150,000 in donations could fund a roughly 100m seawall spanning in front of the pub, the caravan park and the adjoining dune system to the south.

Within four days, more than $40,000 has been raised for the effort from more than 100 donors, with the largest being a $20,000 anonymous donation received off the GoFundMe platform.

Hotel owner Glen Trebilcock said he had long become frustrated by the slow government response to the coastal town’s erosion issue.

“It’s ridiculous, anywhere else and no worries at all, it would have been rectified or dealt with a long time before now,” he said.

“However, WA’s adventure playground has been just left to its own devices.

“It’s definitely something you can’t ignore because further north, you’ve got the caravan park being affected, you’ve got all these people that are looking at buying houses, you’ve got all these sort of single retirees that are saying do we need to sell up now?”

Mr Trebilcock said the seawall had already been designed by coastal and port engineering firm M P Rogers, and would require rocks, core material and geotextile fabric as materials.

A sketch of the seawall, obtained by The West Australian, spans around 100m, shielding the hotel and the southern section of the neighbouring caravan park, as well as some land to the south of the hotel.

The seawall would likely require approval from various authorities departments according to a Shire of Gingin spokesperson.

“Depending on the nature and location of the works, approvals may be required from a range of authorities,” they said.

“In addition to the Shire, the Department of Transport and Major Infrastructure the Department of Planning, Lands and Heritage have roles in assessing and endorsing coastal protection works on the coast.”

When asked if he would wait to get the green light from authorities, Mr Trebilcock said “sure, no problem, if that’s what you’re saying,” while laughing.

Lancelin has been facing accelerated erosion for a number of years, with the State Government providing $150,000 emergency funding in September for replacement sand - which was quickly washed away.

Nationals leader Shane Love said more should have been done months ago.

“It shouldn’t have got to this point, there should have been some proper action taken by Government in the first place,” he said.

“I’ve raised this a number of times in Parliament since the erosion really got underway in this area and we have not had yet any action of any meaningful action, apart from sand renourishment, which is being quickly washed away again.“

A State Government spokesperson said recent storms had meant erosion was exceeding modelling done for the problem.

“The State Government continues to balance the need for timely action with ensuring that decisions are informed by appropriate technical assessment, planning, and approvals,” they said.

“In addition to the $150,000 emergency support provided in 2025, the State Government continues to support the Shire of Gingin through the CoastWA program, which provides funding, coastal data, technical expertise, and planning support.”

The Gingin shire spokesperson said the battle against erosion had not been lost yet.

“The Shire is committed to trying. Whether individual buildings can be protected depends on site-specific engineering,” they said.

“These matters require detailed technical assessment and are not matters that the Shire can determine in isolation.”
